text:
Recent work supports history interventions as tests of recommendation dependence. [Betello et al. (ECIR 2024)](https://iris.uniroma1.it/handle/11573/1706240) found strong sensitivity to removing recent training events, with NDCG declines up to 60% in their experiments; this concerns training-data perturbation, distinct from inference-time attribution. [Scarcelli et al. (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) search for minimal history edits that change sequential recommendations using genetic algorithms. [Spotify’s 2026 benchmark analysis](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) compares transformers with simpler transition-based models, motivating checks of whether apparent sequence understanding reduces to recent-item evidence.

Explanation validation needs known mechanisms and negative controls. [XAI-TRIS (2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10994-024-06574-3) uses synthetic ground truth to quantify false-positive attribution; [EXACT (2025)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2665917424007700) reports that popular explainers can attribute importance to irrelevant features and struggle against random baselines. These are general XAI benchmarks, rather than validated recommender diagnostic suites. A resulting experimental proposal: compare recent-event, recurring-interest and text-boilerplate interventions against controls matched for edit count, position and item popularity; keep candidates fixed and measure paired score, margin and rank changes. Cross-check residual-branch ablations with component gradients, then calibrate detection sensitivity and false alarms using deliberately injected recency-only, popularity-only or boilerplate-dependent scoring faults plus clean controls. These measurements establish model dependence under specified interventions; they do not identify causal user preferences. No searched source established the complete proposed suite as an existing benchmark.
